title: St Bartholomew's Day (1572)
hook: Protestants killed in Paris; religion used for massacre

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vincent de Paul and Louise de Marillac, turning scattered kindness into a plan. Your line was the poor are our masters.

It begins with a wedding. In Paris, the Catholic king's sister marries the Protestant king of Navarre, a match meant to help end years of fighting between French Catholics and French Protestants, who were called Huguenots. Protestant nobles come to the city to celebrate. Soon after, on the feast of the apostle Bartholomew, the killing starts. First the Huguenot leaders. Then neighbors turn on neighbors in the streets, and the violence spreads to other towns. A day on the church calendar, named for one of the twelve, becomes the name of a massacre. This is a hard lesson, and an honest one.

Historians still argue about who gave the orders, and how much was planned and how much was a mob let loose. What isn't in doubt: people were killed for their faith by people who said they shared the same Lord. In the wars of religion that tore at France, both Catholics and Protestants killed, and both were killed. St Bartholomew's Day is the one whose name stuck. And this exact temptation shows up in the Gospels. In Luke, a Samaritan village turns Jesus and his friends away. James and John ask if they should call down fire from heaven to destroy it. In the King James Bible: "But he turned, and rebuked them, and said, Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of." And on the night of his arrest, when one of his followers draws a sword to defend him (John's Gospel names him as Peter), Jesus says, in Matthew: "Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword." His own followers, reaching for violence on his behalf, and both times he says no. That's where today's line comes from: never in his name. It isn't a line about other people's faiths. It's one Christians can turn on their own story, honestly, without pretending it didn't happen. Remembering a day like this isn't about blame across the centuries. It's about recognizing the moment a faith starts to be used as a weapon, so the sword goes back in its place.
screen: `KILLED BY THOSE WHO SHARED THEIR LORD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one place where religion is being used for violence, and don't sort out the blame; just hold the people, the afraid, the grieving, even the ones holding the weapons. If you pray, pray for that place, or rest with put up again thy sword into his place; if you don't, keep it in your attention, with care.
Huguenots. The French Protestants who were massacred first in Paris on St Bartholomew's Day, in a killing that came to stand for faith used as a weapon.
Your line: never in his name. A hard day to remember, and worth remembering. Rest well.

howItsDone: Christians of different churches remember the massacre in histories, sermons and services of repentance and reconciliation, and pray for places where religion is used to justify violence.

notes: Audit: Henry of Navarre was already king of Navarre at the wedding (his mother died that June), so 'a Protestant prince' became 'the Protestant king of Navarre'; Margaret of Valois is described as the king's sister.
Claims rule: the index title's year (1572) is kept in the title field only; the voice gives no date, and the index hook's 'thousands' was cut (no death toll is stated).

Historical frame to confirm: a royal wedding (Margaret of Valois and Henry of Navarre) meant to help reconcile the sides; killing began a few days later on the feast of St Bartholomew, first Huguenot leaders, then mob violence spreading to other towns; historians debate who ordered it.
'Both Catholics and Protestants killed, and both were killed' in the wars of religion: included so neither church is the foil. Confirm the phrasing is fair.
Luke 9:55 in the KJV includes the clause 'Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of', which many manuscripts lack; the script says 'in the King James Bible'. Confirm.
